q: The four values that anchor every contract action?
a: Stewardship · mission · integrity · documentation.
d: Speed · savings · satisfaction · safety.
Competition · compliance · courtesy · closure.
Authority · funding · fairness · files.
x: The guide anchors every action on stewardship (public money), mission (speed matters), integrity (competition and fairness), and documentation (the file tells the story). Each pillar answers a different overseer: the auditor, the warfighter, the public, and the protest.

q: Every action you take should survive which three reviewers?
a: An auditor, an Inspector General, and a protest.
d: The PM, the commander, and the customer.
DCMA, DCAA, and GSA.
The SSA, the SSEB, and the ombudsman.
x: Auditor, IG, protest — the three reviewers who will read your file years later without you in the room. Writing for them now is what 'defensible' means; the PM and commander read for mission, not for compliance.

q: Is "because the program wanted it" ever a complete answer?
a: Never — the file needs the business judgment behind the decision.
d: Yes, when the program certifies the funds.
Yes — the requiring activity owns the requirement.
Only above the SAT does the file need more.
x: The program's desire is an input, never the justification. The file needs the business judgment — market facts, price analysis, competition rationale. Fund certification and requirement ownership don't substitute for the why.

topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
q: PCO vs. ACO — who's who?
a: PCO awards and manages the contract; the ACO (often DCMA) handles post-award administration.
d: PCO handles post-award administration; the ACO awards.
PCO is the specialist; the ACO holds the warrant.
They're the same officer at different dollar values.
x: The PCO awards and manages; the ACO — usually at DCMA — carries assigned post-award administration like payments, mods, and monitoring. Same warrant authority concept, different phase of the contract's life.

topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
q: DCMA vs. DCAA — one line each.
a: DCMA administers contracts and verifies systems; DCAA audits contractor cost/pricing data and rates.
d: DCMA audits rates; DCAA administers contracts.
DCMA runs the schedules program; DCAA certifies funds.
DCMA is DoD's legal support; DCAA audits for GSA.
x: DCMA administers contracts and verifies contractor systems; DCAA audits cost/pricing data and rates. Administration vs. audit — you'll call one for surveillance and the other for numbers.

topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
q: A contractor says "the COR told us to add it." Your flag?
a: Stop and check authority — all contractual direction flows through the CO.
d: No flag — CORs direct technical work.
Bill it as a constructive change and move on.
Ask the COR to confirm it in writing, then proceed.
x: 'The COR told us to' is the classic authority flag — stop and check before more money moves. CORs surveil; they don't direct new work. Even written COR direction doesn't cure the authority gap; it documents it.

q: Express vs. implied authority — the practical difference?
a: Express is written (the warrant); implied reasonably flows from it — both are valid.
d: Express binds the Government; implied never does.
Express is the CO's; implied is the COR's.
Implied requires ratification before it binds.
x: Express authority is the written warrant; implied authority reasonably flows from it (what a CO must do to execute the warrant). Both bind. The invalid lookalike is apparent authority — seeming authorized without being so.

q: An unlimited warrant removes what?
a: The dollar ceiling on the CO's authority.
d: The requirement for legal review.
The clearance gates above the SAT.
The need for a written SF 1402.
x: An unlimited warrant removes the dollar ceiling — nothing else. Legal review, clearance gates, and the written SF 1402 all still apply. That's why unlimited warrants demand deep experience: same rules, no financial guardrail.

q: Two up-front practices that prevent unauthorized commitments?
a: A kickoff meeting, and a letter to the contractor naming who can give direction.
d: A larger GPC program and delegated ordering.
Monthly IG inspections and CO rotations.
Withholding invoices until direction is verified.
x: Prevention is structural: a kickoff meeting that sets expectations, and a letter telling the contractor exactly who can give direction. UACs are trained away, not punished away — repeated ones signal a unit training gap.

topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
q: Rank the rule stack, top to bottom.
a: Statute → RFO → R-DFARS & deviations → DAF policy → local guidance.
d: RFO → statute → DAF policy → R-DFARS → local guidance.
Local guidance → DAF policy → R-DFARS → RFO → statute.
Statute → DAF policy → RFO → R-DFARS → local guidance.
x: Statute beats regulation, the RFO governs government-wide, the R-DFARS supplements for DoD, DAF policy layers under that, and local guidance sits at the bottom. Each layer adds to — never contradicts — the one above.

topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
q: What executive order launched the RFO, and when?
d: E.O. 13876, October 2024.
x: E.O. 14275, 'Restoring Common Sense to Federal Procurement,' April 2025 — the order behind the largest acquisition-rules rewrite in 40 years. E.O. 14402 is the other one you'll meet: contract-type justifications.

topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
q: The DAF's authoritative day-to-day contracting resource — and its catch?
a: The DAF Contracting Compass — it's CAC-restricted.
d: DAU's Adaptive Acquisition Framework — subscription only.
The legacy DAFFARS — being retired.
Acquisition.gov — its DoD content is restricted.
x: The DAF Contracting Compass is the authoritative day-to-day DAF resource — and it's CAC-restricted, which is why public guides can't reproduce it. Public DAFIs (63-138, 63-101/20-101) cover services and lifecycle policy.

topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
q: Which appropriation buys day-to-day operations and most services — and its life?
d: RDT&E (3600) — 1 year.
O&M (3400) — 2 years.
Procurement (3010) — 1 year.
x: O&M (3400) buys day-to-day operations, sustainment, and most services — and lives one year for new obligations. RDT&E gets two, procurement three. Matching the need to the color is the Purpose half of the test.

topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
q: Severable vs. non-severable services in one line.
a: Severable benefits as it's performed (fund ≤12 months); non-severable delivers one end product (fully fund up front).
d: Severable means under the SAT; non-severable means over it.
Severable delivers an end product; non-severable benefits as performed.
Severable is incrementally funded R&D; non-severable is O&M services.
x: Severable services benefit as performed (grounds maintenance) — annual money, ≤12 months, may cross fiscal years. Non-severable delivers one product (a study, an overhaul) — a bona fide need of the award year, fully funded up front.
ref: Field Guide Vol. 1 §5 · GAO Red Book

topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
q: An Anti-Deficiency Act violation is what kind of problem?
a: Obligating more than (or before) funds are available — serious and reportable.
d: A bookkeeping error FM corrects at year-end.
A contractor overbilling issue for DCAA.
Using the wrong CLIN structure on an award.
x: The ADA line is Amount: obligating more than, or before, funds are available. Violations are serious, reportable, and career-relevant — it's the one fiscal statute with names attached to reports. When close to the line, FM and JA first.

q: Order the seven phases of the acquisition lifecycle.
a: Requirement → planning → solicit → evaluate → award → administer → close-out.
d: Planning → requirement → evaluate → solicit → award → administer → close-out.
Requirement → solicit → planning → award → evaluate → administer → close-out.
Market research → award → solicit → evaluate → administer → requirement → close-out.
x: Requirement → planning → solicit → evaluate → award → administer → close-out. The arc is the same at $9K or $90M; only the depth changes. Know the arc and every detail has somewhere to attach.

q: A requirement just landed on your desk. The playbook's first step?
a: Understand the need — what, how much, by when, for whom — and push for an IGCE.
d: Pick the contract type first.
Post a synopsis to gauge industry interest.
Confirm the money before defining the need.
x: Step one is always the need: what, how much, by when, for whom — pressure-tested, with an IGCE. Money, market, and method all come after, because they all depend on what's actually being bought.

q: The customer hands you a conclusion ("only this vendor works"). The trap?
a: Typing it up instead of testing it — your job is to run the steps, not ratify the answer.
d: Slowing the buy — customer conclusions are usually right.
Escalating to the HCA before doing anything.
Rejecting the requirement until it's re-scoped.
x: Customers hand you conclusions — 'only this vendor,' 'use it before it expires,' 'add it to the contract.' The job is testing the conclusion through the steps, not typing it. The seven-step loop IS the fast way; unwinding a bad award is the slow one.

q: SOW vs. PWS vs. SOO — the one-line difference.
a: SOW prescribes tasks; PWS defines outcomes; SOO states objectives for offerors to build on.
d: SOW is for services; PWS for products; SOO for R&D.
SOW states objectives; PWS prescribes tasks; SOO defines outcomes.
They're interchangeable labels for the same document.
x: SOW prescribes the tasks, PWS defines measurable outcomes, SOO states objectives and lets offerors propose the approach. The further right you go, the more competition happens on HOW — and the more the winner's proposal becomes the yardstick.

q: A brand-name requirement needs what?
a: Justification — and often a quick sources-sought reveals real competition.
d: Nothing — brand preference is the customer's call.
HCA approval at any dollar value.
A commercial item determination first.
x: A brand name is a competition restriction wearing a part number — it needs justification. The cheap counter is a quick sources-sought: equivalent products surface, and a risky sole source becomes a clean competition.

q: Match the depth of market research to what two things?
a: The dollar value and the complexity of the buy.
d: Schedule pressure and customer rank.
The NAICS code and set-aside status.
Funding color and fiscal-year timing.
x: Research depth scales with dollars and complexity — a $9K tool takes a catalog check, a $9M system takes sources-sought, industry days, and prior-buy analysis. The documented match between depth and stakes is what reviewers look for.

q: The three CICA buckets.
a: Full & open · full & open after exclusion of sources · other than full & open.
d: Sealed bid · negotiated · simplified.
Full & open · set-aside · sole source.
Competitive · urgent · directed.
x: Full and open; full and open after exclusion of sources (the set-aside lane — still competition); and other than full and open (the seven-exception, J&A lane). Three buckets, escalating justification burden.

q: A wrong exception or thin documentation in a J&A exposes you to what?
a: Protest exposure — the J&A must stand on documented market research.
d: Nothing, once the approving official signs.
An Anti-Deficiency Act violation.
Automatic referral to GAO.
x: A J&A on the wrong exception — or on thin research — is protest exposure, and approval signatures don't cure it. The J&A's strength is its evidence; GAO reads the record, not the rank of the signer.

q: Why does the Government insist on competition?
a: Better prices and quality, a broader industrial base, and process integrity.
d: Because protests are cheaper than J&As.
Mostly to develop small businesses.
To spread workload among buying offices.
x: Competition drives prices down, quality up, broadens the industrial base, and protects process integrity — that's why it's the statutory default, not an efficiency preference. 'We've always used this vendor' is a habit, not an exception.

q: What's a split purchase?
a: Breaking one known requirement into smaller buys to stay under a threshold — a violation.
d: Funding one buy from two appropriations.
Awarding to two vendors to build capacity.
Phasing deliveries across fiscal years.
x: A split purchase breaks one known requirement into pieces to duck a threshold — two $9K swipes for one $18K need. It's a violation at any tier, and the GPC program's most common finding. One requirement, one action.

q: What's a CLIN?
a: A contract line item — a discrete thing bought, with its own description, quantity, price, and funding.
d: The clause list incorporated by reference.
A contractor's labor-category identifier.
The funding document number from FM.
x: CLINs are the contract's skeleton: each discrete item with its own description, quantity, price, and funding. Pricing, invoicing, funding, and mods all hang off the CLIN structure — clean CLINs now save pain at every later phase.

q: The item is commercial — which part's streamlined terms can ride along at most dollar levels?
a: RFO Part 12 commercial procedures.
d: RFO Part 15 negotiation rules.
RFO Part 6 competition exceptions.
RFO Part 49 termination clauses.
x: Commerciality is cross-cutting: RFO Part 12's streamlined terms ride along at most dollar levels — simpler clauses, FFP preference, market pricing. Determining it early is one of the highest-leverage moves in the whole strategy.

q: The two contract-type families?
a: Fixed-price and cost-reimbursement.
d: Commercial and non-commercial.
Competitive and sole-source.
Severable and non-severable.
x: Fixed-price and cost-reimbursement are the two families; everything else is a variation on where risk sits between them. Learn the families and the risk bar before the six-acronym zoo — position is the load-bearing idea.

q: T&M contracts require what two safeguards?
a: A D&F that no other type works, and a not-to-exceed ceiling with active surveillance.
d: A J&A and a DCAA pre-award audit.
HCA approval and monthly invoicing.
An award-fee plan and a QASP.
x: T&M pays hourly rates plus materials — little incentive to control cost. So it takes a D&F that nothing else works, a hard not-to-exceed ceiling, and active surveillance. 'Flexible' for the contractor means open-ended for you.

q: FP-EPA exists for what situation?
a: Long performance periods where a fixed price needs adjustment against a named economic index.
d: R&D too uncertain to price at all.
Foreign military sales only.
Contracts paid in foreign currency.
x: FP-EPA holds a fixed price but adjusts against a named economic index — for long periods where locking a price would just buy inflation padding. It keeps FFP discipline while acknowledging markets move.

q: Price analysis vs. cost analysis in one line.
a: Price analysis looks at the bottom line; cost analysis digs into each element (labor, materials, overhead, fee).
d: Price analysis is for sole source; cost analysis for competition.
Price analysis applies pre-award; cost analysis post-award.
Price analysis is DCAA's job; cost analysis is the CO's.
x: Price analysis judges the bottom line (compare offers, history, catalogs, the IGCE); cost analysis opens the hood on each element — labor, materials, overhead, fee. Competition usually buys you out of cost analysis; sole source usually buys you into it.

q: Reasonableness vs. realism?
a: Reasonableness asks "is it too high?"; realism asks "is it unrealistically low?" (mainly competitive cost-type work).
d: Reasonableness asks "too low?"; realism asks "too high?"
They test the same thing at different dollar thresholds.
Reasonableness is subjective; realism is set by the IGCE.
x: Reasonableness asks 'too high?' — always. Realism asks 'unrealistically low?' — mainly on competitive cost-type work, where a lowball estimate becomes the Government's overrun. Same proposal, two different worries.

q: Best evidence of a fair price when competition exists?
a: The competing offers themselves — comparison of proposed prices.
d: The IGCE, which outranks market signals.
Certified cost or pricing data.
Last year's contract price plus inflation.
x: Adequate price competition is the best evidence there is — competing offers discipline each other. The IGCE is your yardstick, not a trump card; certified data is what you demand when competition CAN'T establish the price.

q: LPTA vs. tradeoff — when does each fit?
a: LPTA when "acceptable" is easy to define and risk is low; tradeoff when paying more for a better solution can be worth it.
d: LPTA above the SAT; tradeoff below it.
LPTA for services; tradeoff for supplies.
Tradeoff when schedule is tight; LPTA otherwise.
x: LPTA: pass/fail acceptability, award to cheapest — best when risk is low and 'acceptable' is easy to define. Tradeoff: pay more when a superior offer earns it — for less definitive requirements. The continuum is a risk dial, not a preference.

q: What must trace perfectly in the solicitation, or a protester will find it?
a: Sections L and M — what you ask for must line up with what you evaluate.
d: The IGCE and the funded amount.
The PWS and the CDRLs.
The synopsis and the award notice.
x: L (how to submit) and M (how you'll evaluate) must trace one-to-one. Ask for what you don't evaluate — or evaluate what you never asked for — and you've authored the protest ground yourself.

q: A timely, complete debrief mostly does what?
a: Prevents protests — it shows the process was fair. Treat it as risk management.
d: Starts the claims clock.
Waives the protester's stay rights.
Satisfies the J&A posting requirement.
x: A timely, complete debrief shows the process was fair — and it's the single best protest prevention there is. Treat it as risk management: an offeror who understands the decision rarely pays counsel to fight it.

q: The default rule on gifts from contractors?
a: Don't accept — the exceptions are narrow; when in doubt, decline and ask.
d: Under $50 is always fine.
Acceptable once per year, per vendor.
Fine if disclosed on your financial-disclosure form.
x: The default is don't accept — the exceptions are narrow and counter-intuitive, which is exactly why 'common sense' fails here. Decline, then ask the ethics counselor; a 5-minute call beats an IG referral.

q: Talking to a contractor about a job while working their action?
a: A serious conflict — disclose and recuse before going further.
d: Fine, as long as the job talk stays informal.
Allowed once you're past the competitive range.
A problem only for warranted COs.
x: Job-seeking while working their action is the revolving-door conflict: disclose and recuse, in that order, before anything else happens. The conflict exists at the CONVERSATION, not at the job offer.

q: A proposal was accidentally cc'd to a competitor. First moves?
a: Stop, preserve the evidence, forward nothing, and call your JA and CO today.
d: Delete it everywhere and note the incident in the file.
Ask the competitor to certify deletion, then continue.
Re-open the solicitation to level the field.
x: Stop, preserve, forward nothing, call JA and CO today. A mis-addressed proposal is a potential PIA disclosure — recoverable if handled loudly and fast, catastrophic if handled quietly. Deleting the evidence converts a mistake into a cover-up.

q: The MPT-to-SAT band carries what automatic posture?
a: Reserved for small business when the Rule of Two is met.
d: Reserved for 8(a) firms first.
Full and open with a small-business preference.
GPC-only, regardless of vendor size.
x: The MPT-to-SAT band ($15K–$350K) is automatically reserved for small business when the Rule of Two is met — the reservation comes from the dollar band itself, not from choosing SAP procedures.

q: Wrong NAICS code — what breaks?
a: The size standard, and with it the whole set-aside analysis.
d: The funding cite from FM.
The synopsis posting requirements.
Nothing — NAICS is statistical only.
x: The NAICS code sets the size standard — who counts as small for THIS buy. Wrong code, wrong universe, wrong set-aside call, and a size protest later. It's a decision worth five careful minutes, not a default field.

q: Who reviews actions for small-business opportunity?
a: The Small Business Professional, coordinating with the SBA.
d: The Competition Advocate.
The COCO.
The SSA.
x: The Small Business Professional reviews actions for small-business opportunity and coordinates with the SBA — your partner on set-aside analysis, DD 2579 coordination, and program questions. The Competition Advocate guards competition; different job.

topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
q: The scope question in one sentence.
a: Would the original competitors have reasonably anticipated this change at award?
d: Is the change under 10% of contract value?
Does the contractor agree to the change bilaterally?
Is there money on the CLIN to cover it?
x: The scope question in one line: would the original competitors have reasonably anticipated this change at award? Anticipated → modify. Not → new work: compete it or justify it. Percentages and signatures don't answer it; anticipation does.

topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
q: Before exercising an option, confirm what basics?
a: Price still fair, funds available, need still real, contractor not excluded, performance satisfactory — with timely written notice.
d: A new IGCE, a new synopsis, and fresh competition.
Just funds — the rest was settled at award.
HCA approval and an updated J&A.
x: Before exercising: price still fair (fresh look), funds available, need still real, contractor not excluded, performance satisfactory — plus timely written notice. The option was evaluated at award; the GATES are about now.

topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
q: REA vs. claim — the certification difference?
a: The DoD REA certification applies above the SAT; the CDA claim certification above $100K — different certifications, different thresholds.
d: Same certification, two names.
Claims certify above the SAT; REAs above $100K.
Only claims ever require certification.
x: Two different certifications: the DoD REA certification (above the SAT, an R-DFARS requirement) and the CDA claim certification (above $100K). Different thresholds, different content, different lanes — conflating them is the classic miss.
